description:
Wesam Saad opens the spiritual gifts chapter by asking where gifts come from, who receives them and why they are given. He distinguishes gifts received at the new birth from natural talents and acquired skills. Training can be useful, but a qualification does not create a spiritual gift. Drawing on 1 Corinthians 12, he stresses that the Spirit distributes gifts according to His will. He describes each believer’s giftedness as a unique blend of capacities, and urges Christians to discover and cultivate what God has given rather than coveting another person’s role. The visibility of a gift does not establish the holiness of its recipient.

The central application is service for the common good of the church and the glory of God. Through 1 Peter 4:10–11, Wesam emphasises responsibility to employ a gift in serving one another, especially within the local body where God has placed a believer. Helping elsewhere remains welcome, provided the local church is not neglected. He also distinguishes ordinary acts of Christian care from the sustained ministry in which a particular gift should be exercised. A hospital illustration shows how abandoning one’s responsibility or pursuing an unsuitable role can harm others. Faithful service through difficulty, rather than prominence, becomes the practical measure of growth.

questions.question: How does Wesam distinguish spiritual gifts from talents and skills?
questions.answer: He describes talents as natural abilities and skills as capacities developed through practice. Spiritual giftedness, in his account, is given by God when a person is born again. Study may help someone serve, but completing a course does not itself prove that God has gifted that person for a particular ministry.

questions.question: Who determines the gift a believer receives?
questions.answer: Wesam appeals to 1 Corinthians 12:11: the Spirit distributes to each person as He wills. He urges prayer for recognition and cultivation of an existing gift, rather than treating a preferred ministry as something earned, bought or demanded from God.

questions.question: Does every Christian receive spiritual giftedness?
questions.answer: Wesam says every born-again believer receives a gift. Not yet knowing what it is, or needing to grow in its use, differs from having received nothing. He therefore encourages believers to seek understanding without concluding that God has withheld giftedness from them.

questions.question: What does Wesam mean by one unique gift that includes several capacities?
questions.answer: He understands the singular language of a gift as each believer’s distinctive combination of gifted capacities, such as teaching, administration, service or mercy. His blended-gift illustration does not require every person with teaching ability to have the same measure or ministry as another teacher.

questions.question: What is the purpose of spiritual gifts?
questions.answer: The passages considered connect gifts with the common good, the church’s edification and service that glorifies God through Jesus Christ. Wesam presents giftedness as a responsibility for helping others, rather than a means of pursuing attention or personal status.

questions.question: Does helping Christians elsewhere replace responsibility to one’s local church?
questions.answer: Wesam says it does not. He welcomes service to other churches and neighbours, but argues that it must not come at the expense of the local body. His family-sharing illustration explains why helping someone elsewhere does not fulfil a neglected responsibility to the people immediately entrusted to one another.

questions.question: May a believer decline ordinary care because it is outside their particular gift?
questions.answer: Wesam rejects that excuse. A person should still reach out to a distressed brother or sister even when that form of help is not their particular giftedness. At the same time, ordinary helpfulness should not become a reason to ignore the gift God has supplied for sustained service.

questions.question: How does the hospital illustration challenge competition over ministry roles?
questions.answer: Wesam depicts every member as both needing care and having a particular responsibility to help others. A person who abandons an assigned role to pursue a more admired one harms those needing their help and those receiving unsuitable service. He concludes that growth is shown by faithful use of a gift through difficulty, rather than by the prestige of the role.
